newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -Australia has the edge over Canada.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -Australia has the edge over Canada.

text.p: Divergent interest rate paths in Canada and Australia offer choosy dollar bloc investors a chance to reap rewards in the coming months, analysts said on Thursday.
With a further rate cut in Australia still possible the outlook is healthy for Australian bonds. But they said Canadian rates are near their lows, making bonds less attractive.

"In Australia there is still room for absolute improvement. For Canada, it is more holding fairly steady levels, possibly with yields coming down a little," said Elizabeth Asfeth, analyst on the sales desk at Williams de Broe in London.
"I wouldn't expect much improvement as such, but also I don't expect the long bond yield to go up much in the near future," she said.
The Reserve Bank of Australia made a surprise cut in official interest rates to 6.0 percent from 6.5 percent on Wednesday, which analysts saw as a bid by the central bank to lift economic activity.

Immediately Australian bonds recovered the ground lost after Friday's sell-off in U.S. Treasuries. However these gains were reversed again on Wednesday as Treasuries dragged global bond markets down amid speculation that Japanese investors might be about to pull out of the U.S. bond market.
Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking here, said the feeling that Japanese investment would taper off would affect all dollar markets.
"The one big thing is the unwinding of short yen and long high-yields on bond markets," said Dick Howard, director of economic research at Julius Baer Investments in London.
"The message over the last week is that when the Bank of Japan does raise rates then all three of these markets (Australia, New Zealand and Canada) could have a really bad patch," he said.
But, he said the background was positive for Antipodean bonds.

"In Australia and New Zealand the economies are still quite weak," Howard said. "I wouldn't say the economy is that stimulative and there is certainly scope for a (further Australian) rate cut. The timing may be more dificult but the economic fundamentals are reasonably supportive."

But some analysts were sceptical of a further cut in Australian rates. Lewis said Australian employment data on Thursday might lead many people to feel the rate cut earlier this week could represent the limit to what the Australian central bank would be willing to do to revive demand.
"So if we have come to the end of the rate cut story in Australia, we should probably look for some curve steepening in the weeks ahead," he said.
He said Canada was a little ahead of Australia in the economic cycle, with limited scope for a further rate cut.

"Short rates are already far below the levels of those in the U.S. and there have been some signs in retail sales data and in employment numbers that the Canadaian economy is beginning gradually to pick up some momentum," Lewis said.
Howard said there was zero value in Canada.
"The Bank of Canada has cut rates to a very low level which is clearly giving the economy a big monetary boost," he said.

Over the next 12 months, he said stronger real growth will push up real yields on Canadian bonds although the trend would be rather to a negative bias than to a huge sell off. "For these markets the positive bond story which has ruled through most of the past year is now over," said Lewis. "It probably makes sense for investors, if they want to remain in dollar bonds to go back to the U.S."
